lessons.title: Separating Business and Personal Money
lessons.body: Many okrika sellers mix business and personal money. This is the fastest way to kill your business. You buy stock with money meant for rent, or you spend sales money on personal needs, and soon you cannot restock. The fix is simple: separate your money. Open a separate mobile money wallet or bank account for the business. Use a different SIM card if possible. Every sale goes into that account. Every business expense comes out of it. Your personal money stays in your personal wallet. If you must take money for personal use, record it as 'owner's draw' and subtract it from profit. For example, if you sell 20 dresses at 50 birr each, that's 1,000 birr. Deposit all 1,000 birr into the business account. Then pay yourself a fixed salary, say 300 birr per week. This way, you always know how much the business has. At the end of each day, count your cash and compare with your sales record. Any difference must be explained. This discipline helps you qualify for loans and grow. Start today: get a separate wallet or account. Label it 'Okrika Business'. Never mix.

lessons.title: Tracking Daily Sales and Expenses
lessons.body: You cannot manage what you do not measure. Every day, write down your sales and expenses. Use a simple notebook or a free app like Wave or Keeper. At the end of each sale, record: date, item sold, quantity, price, total. For expenses, record: date, what you bought (stock, transport, rent, airtime), amount. For example: '15/06/2025 - Sold 3 shirts at 100 birr = 300 birr'. '15/06/2025 - Bought 10 shirts from supplier = 500 birr'. At the end of the day, total your sales and expenses. Subtract expenses from sales to get daily profit. Keep receipts for all expenses. If you use mobile money, the transaction history is your record. At the end of the week, review your notebook. You will see which items sell fast and which don't. You will also see if you are spending too much on transport or airtime. This information helps you make better decisions. For example, if you see that you spend 200 birr per day on transport, consider buying in bulk once a week. Tracking takes only 10 minutes a day but can double your profit.

lessons.title: Budgeting for Restocking and Overhead Costs
lessons.body: A budget is a plan for your money. Without it, you may spend all your profit on small things and have nothing to restock. Start by listing your monthly overhead costs: rent for your stall or storage, transport to buy stock, airtime and data, packaging bags, and any helper's salary. Add them up. For example: rent 1,000 birr, transport 500 birr, airtime 200 birr, bags 100 birr, helper 300 birr. Total overhead = 2,100 birr per month. Next, estimate your monthly sales. If you sell 300 items at average 80 birr, that's 24,000 birr. Subtract overhead: 24,000 - 2,100 = 21,900 birr. From this, you need to restock. Aim to spend at least 50% of your sales on new stock: 12,000 birr. That leaves 9,900 birr for profit and savings. But remember, sales vary. So set a restocking budget: decide how much you will spend each week, say 3,000 birr. Stick to it. If you see a great deal, you can adjust, but always keep enough for overhead. Write your budget on paper and keep it where you see it daily. Review it weekly and adjust based on actual sales.

lessons.title: Simple Profit Calculation and Reinvestment
lessons.body: Profit is what remains after you subtract all business expenses from your sales. Many sellers think all the money in their pocket is profit, but that's wrong. You must subtract the cost of goods sold (what you paid for the items), transport, rent, airtime, and any other business expense. For example, you buy 10 dresses for 500 birr total. You sell them for 1,000 birr. Your sales = 1,000 birr. Your cost of goods = 500 birr. Other expenses (transport, airtime) = 100 birr. Profit = 1,000 - 500 - 100 = 400 birr. That 400 birr is your true profit. Now, reinvestment: use part of your profit to buy more stock or improve your business. A good rule is to reinvest at least 50% of profit. So from 400 birr, reinvest 200 birr into new stock. The remaining 200 birr can be your personal income or savings. If you reinvest consistently, your business grows. For example, if you start with 10 dresses and reinvest 200 birr each week, after a month you might be buying 20 dresses. Track your profit weekly. If profit is low, find ways to reduce costs or increase prices slightly. Never eat your seed capital.

lessons.title: Using Mobile Money and Cash Handling Safely
lessons.body: Mobile money is safe and convenient, but you must use it wisely. In many African countries, services like M-Pesa, Airtel Money, MTN Mobile Money, and Tigo Pesa are common. Register for a business account if possible. Always confirm the transaction SMS before handing over goods. For example, if a customer sends 500 birr, wait for the message that says 'You have received 500 birr from...' before you give the item. Beware of fake messages. Scammers send fake SMS. Check your balance by dialing the code (e.g., *144# for some networks). For cash, keep it in a safe place. Do not carry all your cash at once. Use a lockable cash box at your stall. If you must carry money, split it between pockets or use a money belt. At the end of the day, deposit excess cash into your mobile money or bank account. Keep small change for customers. Count your cash before you leave the market. If you have helpers, set clear rules: only you handle money. If you accept mobile money, have a dedicated phone for business. Never share your PIN. If you suspect fraud, report immediately to your network provider.

lessons.title: Planning for Slow Seasons and Emergencies
lessons.body: Every business has slow seasons. For okrika, sales may drop during rainy seasons, holidays, or when customers have no money. You must plan ahead. During good months, save at least 10% of your profit in a separate savings account or mobile money savings. For example, if you make 5,000 birr profit in a good month, save 500 birr. After six good months, you have 3,000 birr for slow times. Also, build an emergency fund for unexpected costs: sickness, theft, or urgent restocking. Aim for at least one month's overhead costs. If your overhead is 2,000 birr per month, save 2,000 birr as emergency fund. During slow seasons, reduce expenses: buy less stock, negotiate lower rent if possible, and focus on selling existing inventory. You can also run promotions like 'buy 2 get 1 free' to clear stock. If you have a mobile money savings account, you can earn small interest. Avoid borrowing from loan sharks. Instead, join a savings group (like a SACCO or chama) where you can access small loans at fair rates. Plan for emergencies by keeping a list of contacts: supplier, landlord, mobile money agent. Review your plan monthly. With a plan, slow seasons won't kill your business.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Managing Money and Daily Operations in an Okrika Business

In the second-hand clothing trade â known across much of Africa as okrika, mitumba, or salaula â daily cash flow is fast, informal, and easily blurred with household spending. A trader can sell well on Saturday and still be broke by Wednesday. This practical reference gives you the systems, numbers, and habits that separate a business that survives from one that collapses. It is written for the African market: mobile money, bale-based restocking, market-day rhythms, and family pressure included.

Treat every lesson here as an operating rule, not a suggestion. The traders who grow are not the ones who sell the most â they are the ones who know where the money went.

1. Separating Business and Personal Money

The single biggest killer of small okrika businesses is mixed money. When the same pocket, the same mobile wallet, or the same tin holds both school fees and restocking cash, you cannot tell whether you are making a profit. Open a dedicated mobile money wallet (M-Pesa, MTN MoMo, Airtel Money, Orange Money, Wave â whichever is dominant in your market) and use it only for business. Pay yourself a fixed weekly or monthly salary from it. If you must keep cash, use two separate boxes and label them.

2. Tracking Daily Sales and Expenses

You do not need accounting software. You need consistency. Record every sale and every expense the same day, at the same time â for example, at closing. A simple exercise book with columns for Date, Item, Sales, Expenses, and Balance is enough. If you have a smartphone, a free Google Sheet or a mobile-money statement screenshot folder works just as well.

Table 1: Sample daily tracking sheet (one market day)
Item / ActivityMoney In (KSh)Money Out (KSh)Running Balance
Opening float (cash box)ââ2,000
Sold 6 blouses @ 2501,500â3,500
Sold 3 jeans @ 4001,200â4,700
Matatu fare to marketâ1504,550
Bought 10 hangersâ2004,350
Mobile money sale (1 dress)600â4,950
Lunch and waterâ1804,770
Transfer to business savingsâ5004,270
Day total3,3001,0304,270

Format adapted from ILO Social Finance "Making Business Money Work" workbook (ILO, 2019) and the Kenya Financial Education Curriculum (FSD Kenya / Central Bank of Kenya, 2016).

3. Budgeting for Restocking and Overhead Costs

In okrika, restocking is your biggest single cost â often a full bale purchased outright. Budget it as a percentage of sales, not as "whatever is left." A workable split for most small traders is 40â50% restock, 15â25% overheads, 10% savings, 10% reinvestment, and the rest as owner pay. Adjust to your reality, but write the percentages down and stick to them for at least three months before changing them.

Table 2: Monthly budget example â small okrika stall (monthly sales â KSh 60,000)
CategoryTarget %Amount (KSh)Notes
Restocking (bales / bundles)45%27,000Buy graded bales; avoid mixed mystery bales
Overheads (rent, transport, airtime)20%12,000Stall fee, matatu, phone data
Savings (slow season + emergency)10%6,000Separate wallet, not easily withdrawn
Reinvestment (display, signage, scale)10%6,000Racks, mannequin, extra market day
Owner pay (salary)15%9,000Paid weekly or monthly, fixed
Total100%60,000â

Percentage ranges informed by ILO Social Finance micro-enterprise budgeting guidance (ILO, 2019) and the Global Findex 2021 finding that 55% of adults in Sub-Saharan Africa save informally â often without a ring-fenced business fund (DemirgÃ¼Ã§-Kunt et al., World Bank, 2022).

4. Simple Profit Calculation and Reinvestment

Profit is not the money in your pocket at the end of the day. It is:

Profit = Total Sales â (Cost of Goods Sold + Overheads + Owner Salary)

If you sold KSh 60,000 of clothes that cost KSh 27,000, paid KSh 12,000 overheads, and took KSh 9,000 salary, your profit is KSh 12,000. Of that, KSh 6,000 goes to savings and KSh 6,000 to reinvestment â for example, buying a better-graded bale, adding a second display rack, or renting a stall at a busier market one extra day per week. Reinvestment is what turns a stall into a shop.

5. Using Mobile Money and Cash Handling Safely

Mobile money is now the default payment channel for many African traders. Use it deliberately:

  • Use a business-registered SIM/wallet where available (e.g., M-Pesa Business, MoMo Agent/Business).
  • Keep your PIN private â never share it, even with family.
  • Confirm every incoming payment before releasing goods. Fraudsters use fake SMS alerts.
  • Withdraw or transfer large cash the same day. Do not carry bale money home in a handbag.
  • Keep a written or screenshot record of every mobile transaction â it is your audit trail.
â  SAFETY WARNING â Cash and Mobile Money Fraud

Never release goods on the basis of an SMS alone. Fraudsters send fake "You have received KSh X" messages, or reverse transactions after collection. Always open your own mobile money app or dial the official balance-check code and confirm the credit in your own account before handing over clothes. Do not share your PIN, do not accept "help" from strangers at the agent till, and do not keep large cash at the stall overnight. In 2022, mobile money fraud was one of the most commonly reported cybercrimes across East Africa (Communications Authority of Kenya, 2023).

6. Planning for Slow Seasons and Emergencies

Okrika demand is seasonal. Sales spike before school opening, Christmas, and Eid; they fall in the deep rainy season and post-festival weeks. Plan for this by building a slow-season fund equal to at least one month of overheads plus one bale. Keep it in a separate mobile wallet or a locked savings account that you cannot easily withdraw from. Emergencies â illness, theft, a flooded stall â should be covered by the same fund, not by dipping into restocking money.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. â Business and personal money kept in separate wallets or boxes â no mixing.
  2. â Every sale and expense recorded the same day, in a book or app.
  3. â Restock budget set at 40â50% of sales, written down, not guessed.
  4. â Owner salary paid as a fixed amount, not random pocket withdrawals.
  5. â At least 10% of monthly sales moved to a slow-season / emergency fund.
  6. â Every mobile money payment verified in your own app before goods leave the stall.
  7. â Profit calculated monthly: Sales â (COGS + Overheads + Owner Salary).
  8. â Reinvestment decision made monthly, not only when things break.

Further Reading (Free, Official)

  • ILO Social Finance â Financial Education for Micro-Entrepreneurs (free training materials, multiple African languages).
  • World Bank Global Findex Database 2021 â data on savings, mobile money, and financial inclusion in Sub-Saharan Africa.
  • Central Bank of Kenya â Financial Education Resources (downloadable booklets, free).
  • GSMA Mobile Money â State of the Industry Reports (free PDFs, Africa-focused).
  • FAO Agripreneurship & Small Business Tools â free guides relevant to informal traders.

Sources cited: ILO Social Finance, Making Business Money Work (2019); DemirgÃ¼Ã§-Kunt et al., The Global Findex Database 2021, World Bank (2022); Communications Authority of Kenya, Sector Statistics Report (2023); FSD Kenya / Central Bank of Kenya, Kenya Financial Education Curriculum (2016).

quiz.q: Why is it important to separate business and personal money?
options: A) It makes tax evasion easier
B) It helps you track business performance and avoid mixing funds
C) It allows you to spend business money freely
D) It is required by law in all African countries
quiz.explanation: Separating money helps you know your true profit and prevents personal spending from draining the business.

quiz.q: What is an 'owner's draw'?
options: A) A loan from the business to the owner
B) Money the owner takes from the business for personal use
C) A business expense for restocking
D) A type of mobile money transaction
quiz.explanation: Owner's draw is when you take money out of the business for personal use, and it should be recorded and subtracted from profit.

quiz.q: How often should you record daily sales and expenses?
quiz.explanation: Recording daily helps you catch mistakes and know your daily profit.

quiz.q: Which of these is a business expense?
options: B) Paying school fees for your child
D) Buying a gift for your friend
quiz.explanation: Transport to buy stock is directly related to running the business.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a budget?
options: B) To plan how you will spend and save money
quiz.explanation: A budget is a plan for your money, helping you allocate funds for restocking, overhead, and savings.

quiz.q: If your monthly overhead is 2,000 birr and you expect 10,000 birr in sales, how much is left for restocking and profit?
quiz.explanation: Subtract overhead from sales: 10,000 - 2,000 = 8,000 birr.

quiz.q: What percentage of sales should you aim to spend on restocking?
quiz.explanation: Aim to spend at least 50% of sales on new stock to keep your inventory fresh.

quiz.q: What is profit?
options: B) Total sales minus all business expenses
C) Total money in your pocket
D) Total cost of goods sold
quiz.explanation: Profit is what remains after subtracting all business expenses from sales.

quiz.q: If you buy 10 dresses for 500 birr, sell them for 1,000 birr, and have 100 birr other expenses, what is your profit?
What is a good rule for reinvestment?
options: B) Reinvest at least 50% of profit
D) Reinvest only when you feel like it
quiz.explanation: Reinvesting at least 50% of profit helps your business grow steadily.

quiz.q: Why should you confirm mobile money transaction SMS before giving goods?
options: A) To avoid fake payment messages
quiz.explanation: Scammers send fake SMS, so confirming the actual message protects you from loss.

quiz.q: Where should you keep excess cash at the end of the day?
options: C) Deposit into mobile money or bank account
D) Give it to a friend
quiz.explanation: Depositing excess cash keeps it safe and reduces theft risk.

quiz.q: What should you never share?
quiz.explanation: Your PIN is confidential; sharing it can lead to theft.

quiz.q: If you have a helper, who should handle money?
quiz.explanation: To avoid mismanagement, only you should handle business money.

quiz.q: What is a good way to handle cash safely at your stall?
options: A) Keep it in a lockable cash box
B) Leave it on the table
C) Carry all of it in your hand
D) Give it to a stranger to hold
quiz.explanation: A lockable cash box reduces the risk of theft.

quiz.q: Why is it important to plan for slow seasons?
options: A) To avoid running out of money when sales drop
quiz.explanation: Planning ahead helps you survive periods when sales are low.

quiz.q: How much of your profit should you save for slow seasons?
quiz.explanation: Saving at least 10% of profit during good months builds a buffer for slow times.

quiz.q: What is an emergency fund for?
options: A) Buying new clothes for yourself
B) Unexpected costs like sickness or theft
quiz.explanation: An emergency fund covers unexpected business or personal emergencies.

quiz.q: What can you do to clear slow-moving stock during a slow season?
options: B) Run promotions like 'buy 2 get 1 free'
quiz.explanation: Promotions attract customers and help clear old inventory.

quiz.q: What is a savings group (SACCO or chama)?
options: A) A group where you can save and access small loans
C) A type of mobile money
quiz.explanation: Savings groups allow members to save together and borrow at fair rates.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid loan sharks?
options: A) They charge very high interest
quiz.explanation: Loan sharks charge exploitative interest rates that can ruin your business.

quiz.q: What should you do if you suspect mobile money fraud?
options: B) Report immediately to your network provider
C) Tell the customer to send again
quiz.explanation: Reporting quickly can help recover funds and prevent further fraud.

quiz.q: How often should you review your budget?
quiz.explanation: Weekly review helps you adjust to actual sales and expenses.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of tracking daily sales and expenses?
options: A) You can identify fast-selling items and control costs
B) You can avoid paying taxes
D) You can increase prices randomly
quiz.explanation: Tracking reveals patterns that help you make better business decisions.

quiz.q: If you spend 200 birr per day on transport, what could you do to reduce it?
options: A) Buy in bulk once a week
quiz.explanation: Buying in bulk reduces the number of trips and transport costs.

quiz.q: What is the first step in separating business and personal money?
options: A) Open a separate mobile money wallet or bank account
D) Keep all cash in one pocket
quiz.explanation: A separate account ensures clear tracking of business funds.

quiz.q: Why should you keep receipts for business expenses?
options: A) To prove expenses and track spending
quiz.explanation: Receipts provide evidence of expenses and help you calculate profit accurately.

quiz.q: What is a simple tool for tracking sales and expenses?
options: A) A notebook or free app like Wave
quiz.explanation: A notebook or simple app is affordable and effective for record-keeping.

quiz.q: If your overhead is 2,100 birr and you want a one-month emergency fund, how much should you save?
quiz.explanation: One month's overhead is 2,100 birr, so save that amount for emergencies.

quiz.q: What is the danger of mixing business and personal money?
options: A) You may spend business funds on personal needs and fail to restock
B) You will make more profit
C) You will attract more customers
D) You will save more money
quiz.explanation: Mixing funds leads to poor tracking and can cripple your business.
